claim:
Let \(X=(\mathbb R^2,N)\) be the real regular-octagonal Banach plane
\[
N(u,v)=\max\left\{|u|,|v|,\frac{|u|+|v|}{\sqrt2}\right\}.
\]
For the Schäffer nonsquare constant
\[
C_S(X)=\inf_{x,y\in S_X}\max\{N(x+y),N(x-y)\},
\]
one has \(C_S(X)=\sqrt2\). More strongly,
\[
\max\{N(x+y),N(x-y)\}=\sqrt2
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
y=\pm Qx,
\]
where \(Q(u,v)=(-v,u)\) is Euclidean quarter-turn rotation. Hence every Schäffer-minimizing pair is automatically isosceles,
\[
N(x+y)=N(x-y)=\sqrt2,
\]
and the Schäffer minimizers coincide exactly with the James-maximizing pairs in this regular-octagonal plane.

correctness.rationale: Modulo regular-octagon symmetries and the harmless sign change \(y\mapsto-y\), every pair reduces to \(x=(1,t)\), \(0\le t\le\sqrt2-1\), with \(y\) on one of five upper-half boundary pieces. The two vertical pieces give a chord of norm \(2\); the upper-right slanted piece gives \(N(x+y)>\sqrt2\); the upper-left slanted piece gives \(N(x-y)>\sqrt2\) except at its shared top-edge endpoint. On the top edge \(y=(a,1)\), the conditions \(N(x+y)\le\sqrt2\) and \(N(x-y)\le\sqrt2\) are respectively \(a+t\le0\) and \(a+t\ge0\), so equality for the Schäffer objective forces \(a=-t\), i.e. \(y=Qx\). Direct substitution gives both chord norms \(\sqrt2\).
risks: The proof is specific to real scalars and this regular octagon.
The scalar value is known from general identities; correctness of the new result rests on the equality-set exhaustion.

value.rationale: The Schäffer constant is the classical infimal companion to the James nonsquare constant, and the regular octagon is a standard non-Hilbert benchmark with minimal James constant. The scalar Schäffer value is therefore not the contribution; the mathematically substantive point is that every minimizer is forced into the same quarter-turn orbit relation as every James maximizer. Complete equality classifications for canonical nonsquare benchmarks are natural structural data, and this coincidence is not implied by the known scalar identity.
risks: The result refines one canonical plane rather than giving a family-wide classification.
Its value depends on the equality-set theorem, not on the already known numerical constant.
